constraints: each group is non-empty with distinct ids in [0, similarityScores.length - 1]
clarifyingQuestions: How is a group scored: the sum, the average or the minimum of its top k scores?
What if a group has fewer than k movies?
Is the answer a group index, the group itself or its score, and how are ties broken?
hints: Only the k largest scores of each group matter.
A min-heap of size k keeps the current top k while scanning a group.
Sum each heap, and replace the best only when a strictly larger total appears so the earliest group wins ties.
invariants: the heap holds the k largest scores seen so far in the current group
the best index changes only on a strictly larger total
chooseWhen: Top-k selection inside many small groups
tradeoffs: A size-k heap avoids sorting a whole group; sorting is simpler and fine for small groups
hack2hire:68f5af31a269f53ea0eff8a0.variantLabel: Single variant: group with the largest top-k similarity sum

constraints: a plate is 1 to 10 characters from A-Z and 0-9
a checkpoint is 1 to 3 letters A-Z followed by a number without leading zeros, at most 999999999
clarifyingQuestions: Is a vehicle charged between every two consecutive passes, or only between paired entry and exit passes?
Should vehicles seen once be reported with 0?
In which order are the plates returned?
hints: A checkpoint position is the number left after removing the letters from its name.
For each plate you only need its previous position and its running total.
Keep a dictionary plate -> [last position, total]; add 10 * |position - last| on every pass after the first, then sort the plates.
invariants: after processing record i, each plate maps to its latest position among records 0..i
each total is a multiple of 10
chooseWhen: Per-key running aggregates over an event log
tradeoffs: A dictionary pass is linear; rescanning the log per plate is quadratic
hack2hire:677f3733edc5bbd98ac0ea5a.variantLabel: Single variant: total toll per vehicle over consecutive passes

clarifyingQuestions: Must neighbouring values in the non-zero part differ by exactly 1, or only strictly increase and decrease?
Can an element be lowered below zero?
Is an all-zero array bitonic?
hints: Only lowering is allowed, so the cost is sum(arr) minus the sum of the target, and a 1..k..1 block sums to k * k.
A peak k at position c fits when arr[i] >= k - |i - c| for every i in the block, that is k <= arr[i] + |i - c|.
Compute min over i of arr[i] + |i - c| for every c with a forward pass and a backward pass, cap by the distance to both ends, and take the best k.
invariants: left[c] = min(arr[c], left[c - 1] + 1) is the minimum of arr[i] + c - i over i <= c
a peak k fits at c exactly when k <= min(c + 1, n - c, left[c], right[c])
chooseWhen: Fitting the largest pyramid under a skyline
tradeoffs: Two linear passes replace trying every peak and height
hack2hire:677de134052a260e01657068.variantLabel: Single variant: lower elements into a 1..k..1 pyramid

clarifyingQuestions: Must every server in a range get the same x?
Can x differ between operations?
Is the answer the total of x or the number of operations?
hints: Look at each adjacent pair where the power drops.
An operation that starts exactly at i can close the drop before i; an operation covering both servers cannot.
Raise the whole suffix from i by the drop power[i - 1] - power[i]; the sum of all drops is both achievable and necessary.
invariants: after fixing drops 1..i by raising suffixes, the prefix 0..i is non-decreasing
each drop contributes exactly its size
chooseWhen: Range-increment problems that reduce to adjacent differences
tradeoffs: The drop sum is linear; searching over target arrays is exponential and only serves as a check
hack2hire:67873a44e20f8f324213c29a.variantLabel: Single variant: minimal total range increments to sort powers

constraints: a command is "reverseRow r" or "swap r1 r2" with single spaces and in-range decimal indices without leading zeros
clarifyingQuestions: Which other commands exist beyond reverseRow and swap?
Are indices always valid, and can r1 equal r2?
Is the result the final matrix or something derived from it?
hints: Parse each command by splitting on the space.
Swapping rows only changes which row sits where; reversing changes the order inside one row.
Track a row permutation and a reversed flag per row so every command is O(1), and materialise the matrix once at the end.
invariants: position i of the result shows original row order[i], reversed when its flag is set
the input matrix is never written
chooseWhen: Many cheap edits on a structure that is read only once at the end
tradeoffs: Lazy flags make each command O(1); direct application costs O(m) per reversal but is easier to extend with other commands
hack2hire:69a357a36e73e4abccc9bf9c.variantLabel: Single variant: apply row reversals and row swaps

clarifyingQuestions: Must prefix sums be strictly positive, or is zero allowed?
Is the answer the count of minus signs or the sign assignment?
Can a[0] ever be negative?
hints: The first number must be positive, and every later choice only has to keep the prefix sums above zero.
Negate greedily; when a prefix sum fails, some earlier minus must become plus.
Undo the largest negated value seen so far (a max-heap): it restores the most sum for the loss of one minus sign.
invariants: after processing i the running sum is positive
the heap holds exactly the negated values among a[0..i]
chooseWhen: Maximising the count of chosen items under a running-sum constraint
tradeoffs: The heap greedy is O(n log n); exhaustive search is exponential and only a check
hack2hire:67a4d4ca2a9ed767fa215433.variantLabel: Single variant: most minus signs with positive prefix sums

constraints: the time limit is fixed at 60 minutes
clarifyingQuestions: Does "m tasks simultaneously" mean m parallel slots per machine, each running tasks one after another?
Does a task finishing exactly at minute 60 count?
Must tasks run in the given order, or may they be reordered?
hints: Count the parallel capacity: n machines times m tasks each gives n * m slots.
Shorter tasks leave more time, so try them first.
Keep the slot end times in a min-heap; give each task to the earliest-free slot and stop at the first task that would end after minute 60.
invariants: slot end times never exceed 60
tasks are started in non-decreasing duration order, so the earliest free time never decreases
chooseWhen: Greedy assignment to identical parallel workers with a deadline
tradeoffs: A heap gives O(log s) per task; scanning slots is O(s) per task; neither solves the general bin-packing maximum, which the inferred rule does not require
hack2hire:67735a0732f9cd104fc349d4.variantLabel: Single variant: shortest-first tasks on earliest-free slots within 60 minutes

clarifyingQuestions: Is the objective the maximum sum of visited cells?
Does the path end on first entering the bottom row?
Do negative scores occur?
hints: Each move goes exactly one row down, so the best score into a cell depends only on the row above.
best[i][j] = board[i][j] + max(best[i - 1][j - 1], best[i - 1][j], best[i - 1][j + 1]) over in-grid, reachable cells.
Start with only (0, p) reachable, roll one row at a time and return the maximum of the last row.
invariants: best[i][j] is the largest sum of a path from (0, p) that ends at (i, j)
cells farther than i columns from p are unreachable in row i
chooseWhen: Grid paths with local moves and an additive objective
tradeoffs: A rolling row is O(M) memory; enumerating paths is exponential
hack2hire:6a57ce72665efda9311f94c4.variantLabel: Variant 1: best downward path without jumps

clarifyingQuestions: Is the objective the maximum sum of visited cells?
Does the path end on first entering the bottom row?
Do negative scores occur?
Is K a total over the path or a per-row limit?
hints: Add the number of jumps used to the state.
A cell (i, j) with u jumps is reached from row i - 1 with u jumps or from (i - 2, j) with u - 1 jumps.
Fill best[i][j][u] row by row, keep unreachable states out, and take the maximum over the bottom row and all u <= k.
invariants: best[i][j][u] is the largest sum of a path from (0, p) ending at (i, j) that used exactly u jumps
a jump never lands below row N - 1
chooseWhen: Grid paths with a bounded number of special moves
tradeoffs: The extra dimension costs a factor k + 1; enumerating paths is exponential
hack2hire:6a57d29e665efda9311f950a.variantLabel: Variant 2: best downward path with at most k jumps

clarifyingQuestions: Is the objective the maximum sum of visited cells?
Does the path end on first entering the bottom row?
Do negative scores occur?
Which path is returned when several reach the maximum?
hints: Compute, for every state, the best sum still obtainable from it to the bottom row.
A forward walk that only enters states keeping the optimum produces a best path.
The candidate next cells in increasing order are (i + 1, j - 1), (i + 1, j), (i + 1, j + 1), (i + 2, j); taking the first optimal one gives the smallest list.
invariants: down[i][j][r] is the best sum from (i, j) to the bottom row with r jumps still allowed
two different paths first differ in a next-cell choice, so the greedy walk is lexicographically smallest
chooseWhen: Reconstructing a canonical optimal path from a value table
tradeoffs: A backward table makes reconstruction greedy; storing parent pointers needs an explicit tie rule
hack2hire:6a57d9ca665efda9311f954c.variantLabel: Variant 3: reconstruct the best path with at most k jumps

clarifyingQuestions: Is the objective the maximum sum of visited cells?
Does the path end on first entering the bottom row?
Do negative scores occur?
Are two paths with the same cells but different jump counts the same path?
Is the count reported modulo 1000000007?
hints: Count paths per state alongside the best sum.
Merging two predecessor states: a larger sum replaces the count, an equal sum adds the counts.
Do the same merge over the bottom-row states with every jump count; reduce counts modulo 1000000007 after each addition.
invariants: each state stores the best sum into it and how many paths achieve that sum
a cell list fixes its jumps, so states with different jump counts never double-count one path
chooseWhen: Counting optimal solutions of a dynamic programme
tradeoffs: Pairing (value, count) costs the same order as the plain maximum; enumeration is exponential

clarifyingQuestions: Must every parcel belong to some shipment?
What is returned when no split works?
Is "less than the maximum" strict?
hints: A shipment ending at i is balanced when an earlier parcel inside it is heavier than parcel i.
That holds exactly when the shipment starts at or before the nearest earlier heavier parcel, found with a monotonic stack.
Let best[t] be the most shipments covering the first t parcels; best[i + 1] = 1 + max(best[0..g]), and a prefix maximum makes that O(1).
invariants: the stack holds indices with strictly decreasing weights
best[t] is minus infinity when the first t parcels cannot be split
chooseWhen: Partition dynamic programmes with a monotone validity window
tradeoffs: The stack-plus-prefix-maximum is linear; direct segment checks are quadratic
hack2hire:67874b97e20f8f324213c29c.variantLabel: Single variant: partition parcels into the most balanced shipments

clarifyingQuestions: Can the graph contain cycles, unlike LeetCode 1557?
Is the answer the count or the list of servers?
Are self-loops and repeated edges possible?
hints: In an acyclic graph the answer is the number of nodes with in-degree 0.
With cycles, a cycle can be activated through any one of its servers: contract strongly connected components.
Find the components (iteratively, to avoid deep recursion) and count those with no edge coming from another component.
invariants: servers in one strongly connected component reach each other
a source component must contain an activated server, and one per source component suffices
chooseWhen: Reachability covers on directed graphs with cycles
tradeoffs: Tarjan is linear but intricate when iterative; Kosaraju with two passes is simpler; all-pairs reachability is quadratic and only a check
hack2hire:68c4484970268e95f5f43d5e.variantLabel: Single variant: count source components of a directed graph
